statement.p:
In this exercise, we will consider the span of some sets of two- and three-dimensional vectors.
Consider the vectors
\vec{v_1} = \twovec{1}{-2}, \vec{v_2} = \twovec{4}{3} .
Is \vec{b} = \twovec{2}{1} in \laspan{\vec{v_1},\vec{v_2}}?
Give a geometric description of \laspan{\vec{v_1},\vec{v_2}}.
Consider the vectors
\vec{v_1}=\threevec{2}{1}{3}, \vec{v_2}=\threevec{-2}{0}{2}, \vec{v_3}=\threevec{6}{1}{-1}
.
Is the vector \vec{b}=\threevec{-10}{-1}{5} in \laspan{\vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\vec{v_3}}?

Suppose that A is an m \times n matrix. Can you guarantee that the equation A\vec{x} = \zerovec is consistent?
What is \laspan{\zerovec,\zerovec,\ldots,\zerovec}?

Yes, \vec{x}=\zerovec is a solution to the equation A\vec{x}=\zerovec.
\laspan{\zerovec,\zerovec,\ldots,\zerovec} consists only of the vector \zerovec.

statement.p:
For both parts of this exercise, give a geometric description of sets of the vectors \vec{b} and include a sketch.
For which vectors \vec{b} in \real^2 is the equation
\left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 \amp -6 \\ -2 \amp 4 \\ \end{array}\right] \vec{x} = \vec{b} consistent?
For which vectors \vec{b} in \real^2 is the equation
\left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 \amp -6 \\ -2 \amp 2 \\ \end{array}\right] \vec{x} = \vec{b} consistent?

li.p:
\left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 \amp -6 \\ -2 \amp 4 \\ \end{array}\right] \sim \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 \amp -2 \\ 0 \amp 0 \\ \end{array}\right]
so \vec{b} must be on the line defined by \twovec{3}{-2}.

\left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 \amp -6 \\ -2 \amp 2 \\ \end{array}\right] \sim \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 1 \\ \end{array}\right]
so \vec{b} can be any vector in \real^2.
\vec{b} must be a scalar multiple of \twovec{3}{-2}.
\vec{b} can be any vector in \real^2.

statement.p:
Consider the following matrices:
A = \left[\begin{array}{rrrr} 3 \amp 0 \amp -1 \amp 1 \\ 1 \amp -1 \amp 3 \amp 7 \\ 3 \amp -2 \amp 1 \amp 5 \\ -1 \amp 2 \amp 2 \amp 3 \\ \end{array}\right],~~~ B = \left[\begin{array}{rrrr} 3 \amp 0 \amp -1 \amp 4 \\ 1 \amp -1 \amp 3 \amp -1 \\ 3 \amp -2 \amp 1 \amp 3 \\ -1 \amp 2 \amp 2 \amp 1 \\ \end{array}\right] . Do the columns of A span \real^4? Do the columns of B span \real^4?

li.p:
The reduced row echelon form of A is
\left[\begin{array}{rrrr} 3 \amp 0 \amp -1 \amp 1 \\ 1 \amp -1 \amp 3 \amp 7 \\ 3 \amp -2 \amp 1 \amp 5 \\ -1 \amp 2 \amp 2 \amp 3 \end{array}\right] \sim \left[\begin{array}{rrrr} 1 \amp 0 \amp 0 \amp 1 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \end{array}\right]
so the columns of A do not span \real^4.

The reduced row echelon form of B is
\left[\begin{array}{rrrr} 3 \amp 0 \amp -1 \amp 4 \\ 1 \amp -1 \amp 3 \amp -1 \\ 3 \amp -2 \amp 1 \amp 3 \\ -1 \amp 2 \amp 2 \amp 1 \end{array}\right] \sim \left[\begin{array}{rrrr} 1 \amp 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \amp 1 \end{array}\right]
so the columns of B span \real^4.

answer.p: The columns of A do not span \real^4. The columns of B do.

statement.p:
Determine whether the following statements are true or false and provide a justification for your response. Throughout, we will assume that the matrix A has columns \vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\ldots,\vec{v_n}; that is,
A = \left[\begin{array}{rrrr} \vec{v_1}\amp\vec{v_2}\amp\ldots\amp\vec{v_n} \end{array}\right] .
If the equation A\vec{x} = \vec{b} is consistent, then \vec{b} is in \laspan{\vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\ldots,\vec{v_n}}.
The equation A\vec{x} = \vec{v_1} is consistent.
If \vec{v_1}, \vec{v_2}, \vec{v_3}, and \vec{v_4} are vectors in \real^3, then their span is \real^3.

False. The span could be a smaller set.

statement.p: The following observation will be helpful in this exercise. If we want to find a solution to the equation AB\vec{x} = \vec{b}, we could first find a solution to the equation A\yvec = \vec{b} and then find a solution to the equation B\vec{x} = \yvec.

Suppose that A is a 3\times 4 matrix whose columns span \real^3 and B is a 4\times 5 matrix. In this case, we can form the product AB.
What is the shape of the product AB?
Can you guarantee that the columns of AB span \real^3?
If you know additionally that the span of the columns of B is \real^4, can you guarantee that the columns of AB span \real^3?

li.p: AB is a 3\times5 matrix.

No. Since the columns of A span \real^3, then the equation A\yvec=\vec{b} has a solution \yvec for every vector \vec{b}. However, we may not be able to solve the equation B\vec{x}=\yvec if the columns of B do not span \real^4.

Yes. If we are given a vector \vec{b} in \real^3, we can find a vector \yvec such that A\yvec = \vec{b} since the columns of A span \real^3. Since the columns of B span \real^4, we can find a vector \vec{x} such that B\vec{x}=\yvec. Then AB\vec{x} = \vec{b}, which means that B is the span of the columns of AB.

statement.p:
Suppose that A is a 12\times12 matrix and that, for some vector \vec{b}, the equation A\vec{x}=\vec{b} has a unique solution.
What can you say about the pivot positions of A?
What can you say about the span of the columns of A?
If \cvec is some other vector in \real^{12}, what can you conclude about the equation A\vec{x} = \cvec?
What can you about the solution space to the equation A\vec{x} =\zerovec?

li.p: Since the solution is unique, each column of A must have a pivot position. Since there are also 12 rows, each row must have a pivot position as well. This means that the row reduced echelon form of A is the identity matrix.
Since there is a pivot position in every row, the span of the columns of A is \real^{12}.
There is a unique solution to the equation because A has a pivot position in every row and every column.
There is a unique solution \vec{x}=\zerovec.
There is a pivot position in each row and each column.
The span is \real^{12}.
There is a unique solution.
There is a unique solution \vec{x}=\zerovec.

statement.p: As defined in this section, the span of a set of vectors is generated by taking all possible linear combinations of those vectors. This exercise will demonstrate the fact that the span can also be realized as the solution space to a linear system.

We will consider the vectors
\vec{v_1}=\threevec{1}{0}{-2}, \vec{v_2}=\threevec{2}{1}{0}, \vec{v_3}=\threevec{1}{1}{2}
Is every vector in \real^3 in \laspan{\vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\vec{v_3}}? If not, describe the span.
To describe \laspan{\vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\vec{v_3}} as the solution space of a linear system, we will write
\vec{b}=\threevec{a}{b}{c} . If \vec{b} is in \laspan{\vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\vec{v_3}}, then the linear system corresponding to the augmented matrix
\left[\begin{array}{rrr|r} 1 \amp 2 \amp 1 \amp a \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp 1 \amp b \\ -2\amp 0 \amp 2 \amp c \\ \end{array}\right]
must be consistent. This means that a pivot cannot occur in the rightmost column. Perform row operations to put this augmented matrix into a triangular form. Now identify an equation in a, b, and c that tells us when there is no pivot in the rightmost column. The solution space to this equation describes \laspan{\vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\vec{v_3}}.
In this example, the matrix formed by the vectors \left[\begin{array}{rrr} \vec{v_1}\amp\vec{v_2}\amp\vec{v_2} \\ \end{array}\right] has two pivot positions. Suppose we were to consider another example in which this matrix had had only one pivot position. How would this have changed the linear system describing \laspan{\vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\vec{v_3}}?

li.p:
Finding the reduced row echelon form
\left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp 2 \amp 1 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp 1 \\ -2 \amp 0 \amp 2 \end{array}\right] \sim \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp 0 \amp -1 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp 1 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \end{array}\right]
shows that \vec{v_3} is a linear combination of \vec{v_1} and \vec{v_2}. Therefore, \laspan{\vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\vec{v_3}} is the plane defined by \vec{v_1} and \vec{v_2}.
In that case, there would be two equations involving the variables a, b, and c, and the solution space would be a line.
\laspan{\vec{v_1},\vec{v_2},\vec{v_3}} is the plane defined by \vec{v_1} and \vec{v_2}.
There would be two equations involving the variables a, b, and c.
